message.text: `holdsStray` applies `entryLimit` (65,536 entries) and `tipLimit` (256 MiB) to each folder separately. It reads each folder's blobs and stores every judged entry, with its parsed `SharedRecord`, in the handle's `#judged` map. `retire` calls it once per folder in `seen`, inside one call. So the memory one retirement holds is bounded per folder, not per call, and grows with the whole tip.

evidence.snippet: A commit that passes is pushed whatever the tip's totals. A retirement reads only the top level of `changesets/` and the folders it retires, so it works on a tip past any limit, and it is the one call that does. A commit that fails is refused as `unreachable`, and nothing is pushed. Every other write keeps its limit checks.

- A call holds the whole tip in memory. A tip whose records and cells total more than 256 MiB, or that holds more than 65,536 entries, fails every call as `unreachable` until writers dispose of changesets. The byte limit is provisional, on the coordinator's answer of 2026-11-15; [issue #455](https://github.com/melian-agent/melian/issues/455) designs a read that does not hold the whole tip.

| Memory for records and cells | 256 MiB of readable blobs at the tip, `tipLimit`, from the sizes git reports, a blob counted at every path it sits at, and the read stops at those sizes. The limit counts bytes, not the heap, which holds each blob several times over, as bytes, text and parsed objects | `store.test.ts`, "the bytes a tip may hold"; [issue #455](https://github.com/melian-agent/melian/issues/455) |
| Memory for the entries | 65,536 entries, `entryLimit`, checked before any size is read | `store.test.ts`, "the entries a tip may hold" |
| Memory for the listing of entries | 64 MiB, `listingLimit`, a KiB a line on average; git is stopped there, so the list never grows past it | `store.test.ts`, at the cap and one byte past it |
| A tip past either limit | No write of Melian's makes one: a write measures its commit by both limits before it pushes, and again after it rebuilds on a moved tip, and fails as `unreachable`, pushing nothing, when the commit would pass one. Dispose only shrinks the tip, so it works at either limit. A tip past a limit by another route still fails every call, dispose included. A writer on an older build or a push by hand can make one. A writer clears it by hand, removing files such as a changeset's folder in a commit of their own | `store.test.ts`, "the entries a write may leave" and "the bytes a tip may hold" |

explanation.what: `holdsStray` applies `entryLimit` (65,536 entries) and `tipLimit` (256 MiB) to each folder separately. It reads each folder's blobs and stores every judged entry, with its parsed `SharedRecord`, in the handle's `#judged` map. `retire` calls it once per folder in `seen`, inside one call. So the memory one retirement holds is bounded per folder, not per call, and grows with the whole tip.
explanation.whatToDo: Keep a running total of entries and readable bytes across the folders one `retire` call judges. Once the call's total passes `entryLimit` or `tipLimit`, stop judging and report the remaining folders as kept, for example as `strays` or a new `deferred` list, so that the scheduled job retires them on its next run. Also stop storing a retired folder's judgements in `#judged`, or drop them after the decision. Record the resource in the decision's table, as `docs/guidelines/state-git.md` requires.
explanation.whyHere: In the base git record store decision, `tipLimit` and `entryLimit` exist to bound what one call holds in memory: "A call holds the whole tip in memory", "256 MiB of readable blobs at the tip". The new decision says a retirement "works on a tip past any limit". That is exactly the case where the tip's records exceed what one call may hold. A retirement of every finished pull request then reads and keeps every record on the tip, past the limit meant to protect memory.

properties.failureScenario:
A tip passes the 256 MiB byte limit. Base row 65 says a writer on an older build or a push by hand can cause this. Say it holds 2 GiB of records spread over 1,000 changeset folders of about 2 MiB each. The scheduled job calls `retire(await store.folders())` to bring the tip back under.

1. Each folder passes the per-folder checks at lines 238, 243 and 248, so `repository.blobs` reads every blob of every folder.
2. Line 252 stores each entry's judgement, a parsed `SharedRecord`, in `this.#judged`, which outlives each folder's check.
3. One call ends up holding all 2 GiB of records, several times over on the heap as bytes, text and parsed objects. That is about eight times `tipLimit`.
4. The process runs out of memory, the retirement never pushes, and the tip stays past the limit. That is the outcome retirement exists to prevent, and every other call keeps failing.

message.text: `retire` removes a changeset's whole folder, cell and disposal mark included, so a later `add` or `writeCell` recreates the changeset with no incarnation. The new decision calls this wanted: "a retirement undoes a disposal", "a reopened pull request records again from nothing". But the active base port contract, rule 3 of the shared record decision, says "Disposal is permanent: the port has no way to recreate a changeset, since one would need an incarnation every record and writer carries." The new decision's two `Amends:` lines name rule 13's retention and the git store's limit rule. Neither names rule 3, so the head text sets its own standard for behaviour that rule 3 governs.

evidence.snippet:
# The shared record branch retires the records of finished pull requests

Amends: [the shared record decision](2026-11-13-shared-record-behind-a-store-port.md), rule 13's keeping of the live record: the tip keeps open and recent pull requests' records, and a scheduled job retires the rest
Amends: [the git record store decision](2026-11-14-git-record-store-refuses-by-location.md), what a tip past a limit refuses: a retirement is the one call that still works there

`GitRecordStore.retire(seen)` takes changeset names, each with the tree ID its folder had when the caller decided. In one commit it removes each folder whole, cell included, with no mark. A retired changeset is the same as one never written, so a reopened pull request records again from nothing. Retiring a disposed changeset takes its mark too, so a retirement undoes a disposal. That is wanted: a retirement leaves the tip as if the pull request never recorded, and a disposal's purpose, removing a changeset's records from the tip for good, holds once the job has retired it.

- `dispose` first writes a disposal mark to the cell, and `add` refuses a changeset whose cell holds one. Disposal is permanent: the port has no way to recreate a changeset, since one would need an incarnation every record and writer carries.
- It promises no ordering of records, no history, no transaction across records, no secrecy, and no identity for a writer.

The cell holds one small JSON value: the publication lease and the disposal mark. No verdict reads it.

- **Publication's own slots may tie.** A post, status or ledger comment record carries the generation of the lease it was made under, and the one of the highest generation stands in its slot. Two of one generation are settled by the lowest ID. That tie decides which comment Melian keeps, never a verdict.
- `dismiss` works offline, as it does today: it records locally, and the record reaches the store with the host's next add.

explanation.what: `retire` removes a changeset's whole folder, cell and disposal mark included, so a later `add` or `writeCell` recreates the changeset with no incarnation. The new decision calls this wanted: "a retirement undoes a disposal", "a reopened pull request records again from nothing". But the active base port contract, rule 3 of the shared record decision, says "Disposal is permanent: the port has no way to recreate a changeset, since one would need an incarnation every record and writer carries." The new decision's two `Amends:` lines name rule 13's retention and the git store's limit rule. Neither names rule 3, so the head text sets its own standard for behaviour that rule 3 governs.
explanation.whatToDo: Either keep the disposal mark when retiring a disposed changeset (leave or rewrite `cell.json` as the mark), or add an `Amends:` line for rule 3 of the shared record decision and get a maintainer ruling. That ruling should say how records from a changeset's earlier life are kept apart from its new one, for example an incarnation in the cell that records or leases carry. Do not let the head decision mark this as wanted on its own authority.
explanation.whyHere: Rule 3's reason is that records and writers carry no incarnation. A recreated changeset therefore cannot tell records written before the retirement from records written after it. `GitRecordStore implements RecordStore`, so the git adapter now breaks a promise the port makes to every caller. The test 'takes a disposed changeset's mark with it, so an add starts it afresh' confirms the refusal `add` used to give is gone.

properties.failureScenario:
1. A writer runs `dispose(pull-X)`, so the cell holds `{"disposed":true}`.
2. Later, `folders()` lists `pull-X`, which the test 'names each folder … a disposed one included' shows it does, and `retire(new Map([[pull-X, oid]]))` removes the whole folder at lines 269–278, mark included.
3. A host still holds `pull-X` records from before the disposal and adds them on its next add. Base rule 7 says "dismiss works offline … the record reaches the store with the host's next add". Before this change that add failed with `disposed`. Now it succeeds, and the disposed rounds and dismissals count again for any reader of `pull-X`.

The same missing incarnation also breaks a retired changeset that was never disposed:
1. A pull request is reopened and a new publisher takes a fresh lease. The cell was removed, so the lease generation starts again.
2. A stale host then relays an old `post` or `status` record with a higher generation. Rule 4 says "the one of the highest generation stands in its slot", so the old post outranks the new publisher's post.
3. Under the base rule 3 promise, neither step could happen.
